segments.heading: Function `k_write`: NEON write kernel, used for the first touch
segments.text:
- Lines 530 to 850 stand inside the first branch of the `#if defined(__aarch64__)` of line 491. That branch holds the AArch64 kernels. Its `#else` is at line 851.
- The CRB binary holds this branch. The listing shows the `dup` and `stp` instructions of this function [Ref1]. `dup` copies one 8-byte value into both halves of a 16-byte vector register.
- `PLACE(write)` adds the pad of this kernel. `PAD_write` is 0 (line 211). So the function starts at a multiple of 64 bytes: address 0x4a00 in the listing [Ref1].
- `k_write` stores the value `v` to `n` 8-byte words, from the address `a` on.
- In the test each worker calls it once on its whole buffer, directly after the allocation (line 1646). This is the first touch. It happens before the first interval, and it is not timed.
- The kernel table also offers this function as the kernel `write`. No `--seq` list of the test names `write` [Ref4].

`p` is the write pointer. `end` is the first address after the range: `a` plus `n` words. `vdupq_n_u64(v)` builds one 16-byte vector `q` that holds `v` twice. Machine code before the loop: `dup v31.2d, x2` (x2 holds `v`) and `add x1, x0, x1, lsl #3` [Ref1].

- `do`: the loop body runs before the first test of the end.
- Each `vst1q_u64(p + k, q)` stores the 16 bytes of `q` at word `k` after the write pointer. The 16 stores of one loop pass fill 256 B. Each byte is written once.
- gcc joined each two neighbour stores into one `stp q31, q31` instruction. `stp` stores two 16-byte registers, which is 32 B. Here both are the register q31. The machine loop has 8 `stp` [Ref1].

- Line 553 moves the write pointer forward by 32 words, which is 256 B. Line 554 repeats the loop while the pointer is below `end`.
- Machine code of one loop pass: `add x0, x0, #0x100`, 8 `stp`, `cmp x1, x0` and the branch `b.hi`. That is 11 instructions for 256 B [Ref1].
- gcc put the `add` at the start of the loop pass. So the `stp` instructions use the offsets -256 to -32.
- The first touch of a 256 MiB buffer runs 1048576 loop passes (268435456 B / 256 B).
- The binary bw_new of part A holds the same instruction text for its `k_write` [Ref7].

segments.heading: Function `k_copy`: NEON copy kernel (the test does not run it)
segments.text:
- Kernel `copy`: copies `n` words from `s` to `d`.
- Each loop pass loads 256 B with 16 NEON loads of 16 B.
- The `__asm__` statement of lines 580 to 583 has an empty instruction text. It names the 16 loaded vectors as inputs in vector registers (`"w"`).
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run this kernel. No `--seq` list of the test names a copy kernel [Ref4].
16 stores of 16 B to the destination. Then both pointers move forward by 256 B. Machine code of one loop pass: 8 `ldp`, 8 `stp`, 2 `add`, `cmp` and `b.hi`. That is 20 instructions [Ref1].

segments.heading: Hand-written kernels in assembler text: the comment
segments.text:
- From here to line 849 the loop of each kernel is assembler text inside an `__asm__` statement. gcc copies this text into the function.
- The comment names bandwidth.c as the origin of the read loop, the write loop and the copy loop. Each of the three is the body of a macro here (`DEF_ASMREAD`, `DEF_ASMWRITE`, `DEF_ASMCOPY`). So one more line defines the same loop under a second name (an A/A copy).
- One loop pass of each of these three loops moves 256 B. The read loop has 8 `ldp` instructions. The write loop has 8 `stp` instructions. The copy loop has 8 `ldp` and 8 `stp` instructions. Each of these instructions moves two 16-byte registers.
- The size must be a multiple of 256 B and must not be 0. The loop tests the end only after a loop pass. `main` ends the program with status 2 when `--bytes` is 0 or is not a multiple of 256 B (line 2973). It does the same when the size of a `--seq` entry is not a multiple of 256 B (line 2991).
- The comment gives the reason why d8 to d15 are saved once per call. The row of lines 638 to 641 explains it.
- The comment links the parameter `nops` to step B5 of the earlier investigation [Ref10].

segments.heading: Macro `DEF_ASMREAD`: the loop of `asmread`, `read_nop96` and `read_nop256`
segments.text:
- `DEF_ASMREAD(name, nops)` defines one kernel function. The backslash at each line end continues the macro on the next line.
- `k_##name` joins `k_` and the first argument. `DEF_ASMREAD(asmread, 0)` defines the function `k_asmread`.
- Three kernels of the test come from this macro: `asmread` (line 642), `read_nop96` (line 1063) and `read_nop256` (line 1199).
- `PLACE(name)` adds the pad `PAD_<name>` before the function. For these three kernels the pad is 0 bytes (lines 214, 1057 and 1135). So each function starts at a multiple of 64 bytes [Ref1].
- `a` is the start of the range. `n` is its length in 8-byte words. The function returns nothing.
- `noinline` forbids gcc to merge the function into its caller. So the listing shows each kernel as a function of its own [Ref1].

`p` is the read pointer. `end` is the first address after the range: `a` plus `n` words. Machine code: `add x1, x0, x1, lsl #3`, which computes x1 = x0 + 8 × x1. It runs once per call, before the loop [Ref1].

- `__asm__ volatile( ... )` is a gcc statement that holds assembler text. gcc copies the text into the function. The listing shows the instructions in the order of the text [Ref1].
- `volatile` tells gcc to keep the statement, although no later code uses `p`.
- `\n\t` ends one line of the assembler text and indents the next one.
- `1:` is the label at the start of the loop. In the CRB binary the loops of `k_asmread`, `k_read_nop96` and `k_read_nop256` start at an address of 20 modulo 64 [Ref1].

- `%[p]` stands for the register that gcc chose for `p`. In the listing it is x0 [Ref1].
- Each `ldp` loads 32 B from memory into two 16-byte vector registers. `ldp q0, q1, [x0]` puts the bytes 0 to 15 into q0 and the bytes 16 to 31 into q1.
- These 4 instructions load the bytes 0 to 127 of the current block of 256 B into q0 to q7.

- These 4 instructions load the bytes 128 to 255 of the block into q8 to q15.
- One loop pass has 8 load instructions. It reads 256 B, each byte once, in rising address order.
- Nothing uses the loaded values. No instruction of the loop takes q0 to q15 as an input. The next loop pass overwrites the registers.
- The old read kernel `k_oldread` (line 474) differs in this point. Its loop adds every loaded register to a sum: 8 vector adds per 128 B [Ref1].
- The unrolling is part of this text: 8 `ldp` per loop pass. gcc does not change the instructions of assembler text. It only puts register names in the places of `%[p]` and `%[end]`.

- `#nops` turns the second macro argument into text. For `read_nop96` the assembler sees the three lines `.rept 96`, `nop` and `.endr`.
- `.rept N` and `.endr` are assembler directives. The assembler repeats the lines between them N times. With `.rept 0` it writes nothing.
- Result in the listing, between the last `ldp` and the `add`: 0 `nop` in `k_asmread`, 96 in `k_read_nop96`, 256 in `k_read_nop256` [Ref1].
- `nop` does nothing. It loads nothing. So every loop pass still reads 256 B, and only the instruction count of the loop pass grows.

- `add` moves the read pointer forward by 256 B.
- `cmp` compares the pointer with `end`. `b.lo 1b` branches back to the label `1` while the pointer is below `end`. `lo` means lower in an unsigned compare.
- Machine code: `add x0, x0, #0x100`, `cmp x0, x1`, `b.cc`. The listing prints `b.cc` for this branch and names `b.lo` as another name of it [Ref1].
- Instructions of one loop pass: 8 `ldp`, the `nop` instructions and these 3. `asmread`: 11 per 256 B. `read_nop96`: 107. `read_nop256`: 267 [Ref1].
- The end test stands after the loop body. So the body runs at least once in every call.

- These two lines tell gcc which C variables the text uses.
- `[p] "+r"(p)`: `p` is in a general register. The text reads it and changes it.
- `[end] "r"(end)`: `end` is an input in a general register. In the listing it is x1 [Ref1].

- The last list is the clobber list. It tells gcc what the text changes besides `p`: the vector registers v0 to v15 and the condition flags (`"cc"`). `"memory"` says that the text accesses memory that no operand names.
- v8 to v15 are in the list. So gcc saves d8 to d15 on the stack before the loop (4 `stp` instructions) and loads them back after it (4 `ldp` instructions) [Ref1].
- This save runs once per call of the kernel, not once per loop pass.
- In a timed interval of the test one call covers one 2 MiB chunk (line 1695). That is 8192 loop passes.
- `k_asmread` has 21 instructions: 5 before the loop, 11 in the loop and 5 after it, with `ret` as the last one [Ref1].

segments.heading: `DEF_ASMREAD(asmread, 0)`: the kernel `asmread` of the test
segments.text:
- Defines `k_asmread`, the kernel `asmread`: the macro loop with 0 `nop`. One loop pass has 8 `ldp` loads of 32 B, `add`, `cmp` and the branch. That is 11 instructions per 256 B [Ref1].
- The test runs it at position 1 in part L and control I. In part C it runs at position 2 (cfwd.spec) or position 0 (crev.spec) [Ref4].
- The worker calls it through the function `call` (line 1491). Before each interval of this kernel one call covers the whole buffer: the warm-up pass (line 1669). In the timed interval one call covers one 2 MiB chunk (line 1695).
- The instruction text of `k_asmread` equals the text of `k_asmread` in bw_new, the binary of part A [Ref7].
- `k_read` (line 501), the new read kernel, has the same 8 `ldp` loads and the same count of 11 instructions per 256 B [Ref1].
- The two functions differ in four points. Register numbers: q0 to q15 here, q31 to q16 in `k_read`. Save of d8 to d15, outside the loop: only here. Loop start: 20 modulo 64 here, 36 in `k_read`. End test: `cmp x0, x1` with `b.cc` here, `cmp x1, x0` with `b.hi` in `k_read` [Ref1]. Both end tests branch back while the pointer is below `end`.

segments.heading: `asmread2` and `read_nop4` to `read_nop32` (not run by the test)
segments.text:
- `asmread2`: the A/A copy of `asmread`. The listing shows the same instruction text for both [Ref1].
- `read_nop4`, `read_nop8`, `read_nop16`, `read_nop32`: the asmread loop with 4, 8, 16 or 32 `nop` per loop pass.
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of these five kernels [Ref4].

segments.heading: Function `k_read_sparse` (the test does not run it)
segments.text:
- Kernel `read_sparse`: a read loop of 128 B per loop pass with 4 `ldp`, 9 `nop`, `add`, `cmp` and `b.lo`. That is 16 instructions per 128 B [Ref1].
- The comment gives the aim: the instruction count of the old read loop, without its vector adds.
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run this kernel [Ref4].

segments.heading: Macro `DEF_ASMWRITE`: `asmwrite` and `asmwrite2` (not run by the test)
segments.text:
- A hand-written write loop. `dup` copies `v` into both halves of v0. Each loop pass stores 256 B with 8 `stp q0, q0` instructions.
- Lines 695 and 696 define `k_asmwrite` and its A/A copy `k_asmwrite2`.
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs neither of them [Ref4]. The first touch uses `k_write` (line 531), not this loop.

segments.heading: Macro `DEF_ASMCOPY`: `asmcopy` and `asmcopy2` (not run by the test)
segments.text:
- A hand-written copy loop. Each loop pass loads 256 B from `s` with 8 `ldp` and stores them to `d` with 8 `stp`. Then both pointers move forward by 256 B.
- Lines 733 and 734 define `k_asmcopy` and its A/A copy `k_asmcopy2`.
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs neither of them [Ref4].

segments.heading: Function `k_asmcopy_c` (the test does not run it)
segments.text:
- Kernel `asmcopy_c`, from step B2 of the earlier investigation [Ref10].
- The comment says where its assembler text comes from: it repeats the machine code that gcc made for the C copy loop `k_copy` of the binary bw_new.
- In the listing of bwx12, `k_asmcopy_c` and `k_copy` have the same instruction text [Ref1].
- `register ... __asm__("x0")` binds a C variable to the named register.
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run this kernel [Ref4].

segments.heading: Function `k_asmcopy_c_add` (the test does not run it)
segments.text: Kernel `asmcopy_c_add`: the loop of `asmcopy_c` in another order. The two `add` instructions stand after the 8 `stp`. The `stp` offsets are 0 to 224. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run this kernel [Ref4].

segments.heading: Function `k_asmcopy_c_reg` (the test does not run it)
segments.text: Kernel `asmcopy_c_reg`: the loop of `asmcopy_c` with the registers q0 to q15 in place of q31 to q16. The clobber list names v8 to v15. So gcc saves d8 to d15 once per call [Ref1]. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run this kernel [Ref4].

segments.heading: Stand-ins for other machines (not in the CRB binary)
segments.text:
- `#else` belongs to the `#if defined(__aarch64__)` of line 491. The compiler reads the lines 852 to 896 only for a machine that is not AArch64.
- The CRB binary does not hold this code. Line 2 of every csv file of the test says `kernels=aarch64` [Ref5]. The program prints this word when `STANDIN` is 0 (line 3024).
- `STANDIN` is 1 in this branch. It is 0 in the AArch64 branch (line 492).

- The three macro names of the AArch64 branch, here with plain C loops over the same range.
- `DEF_ASMREAD` reads every word through a `volatile` pointer. It does not use `nops`.
- `DEF_ASMWRITE` stores `v` to every word. `DEF_ASMCOPY` copies word by word.
- Not compiled for CRB.

These lines define all 17 kernels of lines 500 to 849 from the stand-in macros. The 17 include `k_read`, `k_write` and `k_copy`. `#endif` (line 897) closes the `#if` of line 491. Not compiled for CRB.

segments.heading: Kernels added by the version bwx10: the comment
segments.text:
- `/* bwx10+ */` opens the text that the version bwx10 added. `/* bwx10- */` (line 1040) closes it.
- "Round 3" in this comment is a step of the earlier investigation of 2026-11-15 (file comment, lines 61 to 83). It is not a round of `--rounds`.
- The new kernels stand after the older ones. The comment gives the reason: the older kernels keep their place in the binary.
- The planned loop start of every new kernel is 20 modulo 64, the loop offset of `asmread`.
- The four read_pf kernels (`read_pf256` to `read_pf2048`, lines 979 to 982) save d8 to d15, as `asmread` does. So 20 bytes of code stand before their loop, and they take the pad of `asmread`.
- `read_1pl` saves nothing. So 4 bytes of code stand before its loop. The comment calls this number a guess. The listing of the CRB build confirms it (row of lines 923 to 930).

- The pads of the four read_pf kernels. Each one takes `PAD_asmread`, which is 0.
- `#ifndef` lets a `-D` option of the compiler give another value. The CRB build has no `-D` option [Ref2].
- The test does not run these kernels.

segments.heading: Placement of `read_1pl`
segments.text:
- `LOOP_read_1pl` is 20: the planned address of the loop start, modulo 64.
- `HEAD_read_1pl` is 4: the number of bytes between the function start and the loop start. That is one instruction of 4 bytes.
- `PAD_read_1pl` is `PADOF(20, 4)`. `PADOF` (line 164) computes (20 - 4) modulo 64, which is 16.
- `PLACE(read_1pl)` (line 987) uses this pad. So the function starts at 16 modulo 64.
- Listing of the CRB build: `k_read_1pl` starts at 0x55d0, which is 16 modulo 64. Its loop starts at 0x55d4, which is 20 modulo 64 [Ref1].
- So `read_1pl` has the same loop offset as `asmread`, `read_nop96` and `read_nop256`: 20.

segments.heading: Macro `DEF_READ_PF`: asmread with prefetches (not run by the test)
segments.text:
- `#if defined(__aarch64__)` (line 931) opens a second block of AArch64 kernels. Its `#else` is at line 1005. The CRB binary holds this first branch: the listing shows the `prfm` and `ldr` instructions of its kernels [Ref1].
- The comment describes the read_pf kernels: the asmread loop plus four prefetch instructions per loop pass, one per 64 B line. A line here is a block of 64 B of memory (a cache line).
- A prefetch instruction (`prfm pldl1keep`) asks the CPU to bring a 64 B line into the first-level data cache. It loads no data into a register.
- `d0` is the byte offset of the first prefetched 64 B line from the start of the block that the loop pass loads.

- The macro is the text of `DEF_ASMREAD` with four `prfm` instructions in place of the `nop` line.
- `_Static_assert` stops the compilation when the four offsets break the rule of the comment.
- Lines 979 to 982 define `read_pf256`, `read_pf512`, `read_pf1024` and `read_pf2048`. The number in the name is `d0` in bytes.
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of these four kernels [Ref4].

segments.heading: Function `k_read_1pl`: one 16 B load per 64 B line
segments.text:
- Defines the kernel `read_1pl`. The test runs it at position 4, the last position, in part L and control I. Part C does not run it [Ref4].
- The name means one load per line. Here a line is a block of 64 B of memory (a cache line).
- `PLACE(read_1pl)` adds a pad of 16 bytes (line 928). The function starts at 16 modulo 64 [Ref1].
- `a` is the start of the range. `n` is its length in 8-byte words. The function returns nothing. `noinline` forbids gcc to merge it into its caller.
`p` is the read pointer. `end` is the first address after the range. Machine code: `add x1, x0, x1, lsl #3`. It is the only instruction before the loop [Ref1].
The loop is assembler text, as in `DEF_ASMREAD` (line 622). `1:` is the label at the start of the loop. In the CRB binary the loop starts at an address of 20 modulo 64 [Ref1].

- Each `ldr q` loads 16 B from memory into one vector register. The four loads read at the byte offsets 0, 64, 128 and 192 of the current block of 256 B.
- So one loop pass loads 64 B of its block of 256 B: the bytes 0 to 15 of each 64 B line. It does not load the other 48 B of a 64 B line.
- `asmread` has 8 load instructions of 32 B per loop pass. This kernel has 4 load instructions of 16 B per loop pass.
- Nothing uses the loaded values. No instruction of the loop takes q0 to q3 as an input.

- `add` moves the read pointer forward by 256 B. `cmp` and `b.lo 1b` repeat the loop while the pointer is below `end`.
- Machine code of one loop pass: 4 `ldr`, `add x0, x0, #0x100`, `cmp x0, x1` and `b.cc`. That is 7 instructions per block of 256 B [Ref1].
- The worker counts the bytes outside the kernel. It adds the full chunk size, 2097152 B, for each call (line 1696).
- So the rate of `read_1pl` counts 256 B per loop pass, although the loop pass loads 64 B.

- `p` is read and changed. `end` is an input.
- Of the vector registers, the clobber list names only v0 to v3. The calling rules do not require a function to keep these registers. So gcc saves nothing.
- The whole function has 9 instructions: 1 before the loop, 7 in the loop, then `ret` [Ref1].
- `asmread` differs here: it saves d8 to d15 and loads them back at each call.

segments.heading: Stand-ins of the bwx10 kernels (not in the CRB binary)
segments.text:
- `#else` of the `#if` of line 931. The compiler reads these lines only for a machine that is not AArch64.
- The four read_pf kernels become the stand-in loop of `asmread`.
- The stand-in of `read_1pl` reads the first two words (16 B) of every 8 words (64 B).
- `#endif` (line 1022) closes the block. The CRB binary does not hold this code [Ref5].

segments.heading: Pad after the kernels of bwx10
segments.text:
- This comment explains the lines 1036 to 1039. They place the code that follows the kernels.
- Aim: the first function after the kernels starts at 24 modulo 64, as in the older runner bwx8. That function is `call`, or `read_smaps` when gcc merges `call` into its callers.
- In bwx12 more kernels follow this pad (from line 1043 on). So this pad does not stand directly before `call` any more. A later pad with the same value does that (lines 1446 to 1449).
- The build record of CRB reports `call=24`: the function `call` starts at 24 modulo 64 [Ref2].
- `timed_sequence` in the comment is a function of the trial mode. The test does not use the trial mode.

- `PAD_after_kernels` is 24. A `-D` option could give another value, and the CRB build has none [Ref2].
- `PLACE(after_kernels)` fills the code up to a multiple of 64 bytes and then adds 24 bytes of value 0.
- `/* bwx10- */` closes the text of the version bwx10.
- `/* bwx11+ */` opens the text that the version bwx11 added. That text starts after line 1042 with the kernels `read_nop64`, `read_nop96` and `read_nop128`.
